title: The history of the yawn
tagline: From a Greek theory of trapped air to yawning lions and budgies: how people figured out why we yawn.
intro: For two thousand years, yawning was explained as air, fever or a lack of oxygen. In the 1980s simple experiments showed it was not about oxygen at all, and ultrasound found yawns before birth. Since then researchers have studied why yawns spread, why brain size predicts yawn length, and whether a yawn cools the brain. The last question is still debated.

eras.name: Air, fever and humours
eras.summary: For two thousand years, doctors and religious traditions saw the yawn as air, fever, or something to hold back and cover.

eras.name: The nervous system takes over
eras.summary: Doctors notice paralysed arms moving in a yawn and start to see it as a stretch run by the brainstem, not a breath.

eras.name: Stopwatches, gas masks and scans
eras.summary: Ultrasound finds yawns before birth, and lab tests time the yawn and reject the oxygen myth.

eras.name: Catching yawns
eras.summary: Researchers learn who catches yawns, from four-year-olds to chimps, dogs, budgies and lions, and argue about empathy.

eras.name: A brain cooler?
eras.summary: Cold packs, hot summers and brain sizes test the idea that a yawn helps cool the brain.

events.title: A Greek medical text blames yawning on trapped air
events.who: Hippocratic writers
events.text: The Hippocratic treatise On Winds (De flatibus) is the oldest known medical writing on yawning. It says yawning is built-up air rising and escaping through the mouth. It links yawning to fever.
events.why: This air-and-fever idea shaped medicine for about 2,000 years.

events.title: Pliny links yawning to danger
events.who: Pliny the Elder
events.text: The Roman writer Pliny the Elder noted that repeated yawning with heavy bleeding could signal that death was near. Galen and Celsus later built on the Hippocratic wind idea.
events.why: Yawning became a sign doctors watched for at the bedside.

events.title: Hadith collections give advice on yawning
events.who: al-Bukhari and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (compilers)
events.where: Central Asia and the Islamic world
events.text: Two major Sunni hadith collections record sayings of the Prophet Muhammad about yawning. One says yawning is from Satan, so a person should hold it back as far as they can. Another says to cover the mouth with the hand when yawning.
events.why: It is one of the oldest written customs about yawning, and it gave covering the mouth a religious meaning.

events.title: Fernel calls yawning a short fever
events.who: Jean Fernel
events.text: The French physician Jean Fernel (1497–1558) described yawning as an "ephemeral fever". He saw it as a warning sign that came before a feverish illness. He still explained it with the old theory of humours.
events.why: He tied yawning to body heat, an idea that returned in a new form centuries later.

events.title: The oxygen idea is born
events.who: Johannes de Gorter
events.text: In 1755 Johannes de Gorter linked yawning to faster blood flow and a brain short of blood. Albrecht von Haller soon tied yawning to breathing and blood flow through the lungs. These ideas grew into the belief that yawning brings more oxygen to the brain.
events.why: The oxygen belief lasted for about two centuries and is still repeated today.

events.title: A paralysed arm moves during a yawn
events.who: Erasmus Darwin
events.text: In his book Zoonomia, Erasmus Darwin described people with one-sided paralysis whose weak arm moved when they yawned.
events.why: It hinted that yawning runs on deep, automatic circuits in the nervous system.

events.title: Charles Darwin notes tears in a yawn
events.who: Charles Darwin
events.text: While gathering material for The Expression of the Emotions (1872), Darwin wrote a note that tears came into his son George's eyes when yawning. He thought the eye muscles squeezed shut during the violent yawn.
events.why: Darwin treated the yawn as a full-body action worth studying, not just a breath.

events.title: A patient who yawned 480 times an hour
events.who: Jean-Martin Charcot
events.text: The neurologist Charcot presented a 17-year-old patient who yawned about 480 times an hour. He linked it to hysteria and a brain short of oxygen. Walusinski later suggested a pituitary tumour was the more likely cause.
events.why: Odd yawning became a clue in brain medicine.

events.title: Yawning is called a stretch, not a breath
events.who: Dumpert and Claparède
events.text: Dumpert in 1921 and Édouard Claparède in 1924 argued that yawning is part of a stretching reflex. They did not see it as a breathing act.
events.why: It started the idea that a yawn is a movement program, like a stretch.

events.title: Walshe sees paralysed arms rise in a yawn
events.who: Sir Francis Walshe
events.text: The British neurologist Francis Walshe noted that when people paralysed on one side by a stroke yawn, the paralysed arm can rise and bend on its own. The patients were startled by it.
events.why: It showed that yawning uses brain pathways that work even when voluntary movement is lost.

events.title: A review points to the brainstem
events.who: A. P. Heusner
events.text: Heusner reviewed what was known about yawning in Physiological Reviews. He proposed that the brainstem and basal ganglia control it.
events.why: Yawning was now seen as something run by old, deep parts of the brain.

events.title: X-rays show the throat opening wide
events.who: Jacques Barbizet
events.text: Barbizet published a paper titled simply "Yawning" in a British neurology journal. Using X-ray viewing, he found that the throat and voice box widen to about four times their resting size at the peak of a yawn.
events.why: It measured what happens inside the head during a yawn for the first time.

events.title: Ultrasound catches yawns before birth
events.who: J. I. P. de Vries, G. H. A. Visser and H. F. R. Prechtl
events.text: Ultrasound studies of fetal movement found that babies yawn in the womb. Yawning appears by the end of the first trimester, around 11 to 15 weeks, and often comes with stretching.
events.why: Yawning is one of the earliest behaviours a human body shows.

events.title: A stopwatch study of the yawn
events.who: Robert Provine
events.where: University of Maryland, Baltimore County, USA
events.text: Provine had volunteers think about yawning and press a button for the length of each yawn. A yawn lasted about six seconds on average. Once started it ran to the end, like a sneeze, so he called it a fixed action pattern.
events.why: It turned yawning into something people could measure in a lab.

events.title: Seeing a yawn triggers a yawn
events.who: Robert Provine
events.where: University of Maryland, Baltimore County, USA
events.text: Volunteers watched five minutes of a man yawning. 55% yawned, against 21% who watched smiles. Faces with the mouth hidden still worked, so it is the whole face that sets off the yawn.
events.why: It gave contagious yawning its first hard numbers.

events.title: Gas tests sink the oxygen myth
events.who: Robert Provine, B. C. Tate and L. Geldmacher
events.where: University of Maryland, Baltimore County, USA
events.text: Students breathed normal air, pure oxygen, or air with 3% or 5% carbon dioxide. Extra carbon dioxide made them breathe much faster, but they did not yawn more. Pure oxygen did not stop yawns. Exercise that nearly doubled breathing did not change yawning either.
events.why: Breathing and yawning turned out to be separate systems, so yawning is probably not about oxygen.

events.title: Young children do not catch yawns
events.who: James R. Anderson and Pauline Meno
events.text: The team tested 87 children aged 2 to 11 with yawning videos and a yawning story. Children under 5 did not catch yawns from the videos. Older children caught them more and more with age.
events.why: Contagious yawning develops years after the first yawns in the womb.

events.title: Yawn catching is linked to thinking about others
events.who: Steven Platek, Gordon Gallup Jr. and colleagues
events.where: State University of New York at Albany and Drexel University, USA
events.text: Platek's team found that people with more schizotypal traits, who find it harder to read others' minds, caught fewer yawns. A 2005 brain scan study found activity in areas used for thinking about the self and others.
events.why: It started the long debate about yawning and empathy.

events.title: Chimpanzees catch yawns from video
events.who: James R. Anderson, Masako Myowa-Yamakoshi and Tetsuro Matsuzawa
events.where: University of Stirling (Scotland), University of Shiga Prefecture and Kyoto University (Japan)
events.text: Six adult female chimpanzees watched videos of chimps yawning or making other mouth movements. Two of the six yawned clearly more after the yawning videos.
events.why: It was the first sign that another species catches yawns too.

events.title: Reading about yawns makes people yawn
events.who: Robert Provine
events.text: In a review for American Scientist, Provine reported that 30% of people who read about yawning for five minutes yawned. Only 11% did after reading about hiccups. Just thinking about yawning made 88% yawn within 30 minutes.
events.why: Even words can trigger the yawn program.

events.title: Monkeys yawn more at yawn videos, but why?
events.who: A. Paukner and James R. Anderson
events.text: Twenty-two stumptail macaques yawned more while watching yawn clips. But the clips also made them scratch more, so tension might explain it.
events.why: It showed how hard it is to tell true contagion from stress.

events.title: The brain-cooling idea is tested
events.who: Andrew C. Gallup and Gordon G. Gallup Jr.
events.where: University at Albany, New York, USA
events.text: Volunteers watched videos of people yawning. About half yawned if they breathed normally or through the mouth. People who breathed only through the nose, or held a cold pack to the forehead, did not yawn. Warm or room-temperature packs made no difference.
events.why: It launched the idea that yawning helps cool the brain.

events.title: Children with autism catch fewer yawns
events.who: Atsushi Senju, Makiko Maeda, Toshikazu Hasegawa and colleagues
events.where: Birkbeck, University of London, and University of Tokyo
events.text: Typical children yawned more at yawning videos than at control videos. Children with autism did not. The authors suggested a link to empathy.
events.why: It made yawning a test case in autism research.

events.title: Dogs catch human yawns
events.who: Ramiro Joly-Mascheroni, Atsushi Senju and Alex Shepherd
events.text: A stranger yawned in front of 29 dogs. 21 of them, or 72%, yawned too. None yawned when the person only opened and closed the mouth.
events.why: Yawns can jump between species.

events.title: Gelada monkeys catch yawns from close friends
events.who: Elisabetta Palagi and colleagues
events.text: Researchers recorded 3,229 yawns in gelada monkeys. Yawns spread most between animals that groomed each other often. Adult females even copied the type of yawn they saw.
events.why: Emotional closeness, not just distance, predicted who caught a yawn.

events.title: Age four is the turning point
events.who: Molly Helt, Inge-Marie Eigsti, Peter Snyder and Deborah Fein
events.text: Among 120 children aged 1 to 6, almost none under 4 caught a yawn. At age four, 7 of 20 did. Children with autism caught yawns about half as often as other children.
events.why: It pinned down when contagious yawning appears in childhood.

events.title: Rat brains cool after a yawn
events.who: M. L. Shoup-Knox, A. C. Gallup, G. G. Gallup Jr. and E. C. McNay
events.text: Sensors in rats' brains showed temperature rising just before yawns and stretches. After a yawn the brain cooled by about 0.11 °C on average.
events.why: It was direct evidence linking yawns to brain temperature.

events.title: People yawn less in hot Arizona summers
events.who: Andrew C. Gallup and Omar T. Eldakar
events.text: Pedestrians looked at pictures of people yawning. In winter, at about 22 °C, 45% yawned. In early summer, at about 37 °C, only about 24% did.
events.why: When air is as warm as the body, a yawn cannot cool the brain, so the theory predicted fewer yawns.

events.title: Chimps catch yawns from their own group
events.who: Matthew W. Campbell and Frans B. M. de Waal
events.where: Yerkes National Primate Research Center, Emory University, USA
events.text: Twenty-three chimpanzees watched videos. They yawned more when familiar group members yawned than when strangers yawned.
events.why: It added to the evidence that social ties shape contagion.

events.title: We catch yawns most from family
events.who: Ivan Norscia and Elisabetta Palagi
events.text: The team watched 109 adults in everyday places such as workplaces and restaurants. Yawns spread most between relatives, then friends, then acquaintances, and least between strangers.
events.why: Closeness, not just seeing a yawn, sets how catching it is.

events.title: 4D scans track fetal yawns
events.who: Nadja Reissland, Brian Francis and James Mason
events.where: Durham University and Lancaster University, England
events.text: The team scanned 15 healthy fetuses four times between 24 and 36 weeks. They told yawns apart from other mouth openings by timing: a yawn opens slowly and closes fast. Both became less frequent as the fetus grew.
events.why: It gave doctors a way to tell a real fetal yawn from a simple mouth opening.

events.title: Measuring the body during a yawn
events.who: T. P. Corey, M. L. Shoup-Knox, E. B. Gordis and G. G. Gallup Jr.
events.text: Volunteers wore sensors while they yawned. Heart rate rose at the yawn's peak and just after. Lung volume peaked at the top of the yawn, and eye muscles tightened.
events.why: It showed a yawn changes heart, lungs and face all at once.

events.title: Dogs catch their owners' yawns more
events.who: Teresa Romero, Akitsugu Konno and Toshikazu Hasegawa
events.text: Twenty-five pet dogs yawned more when their owner yawned than when a stranger did. Their heart rates did not suggest stress.
events.why: It linked yawn contagion in dogs to social bonds.

events.title: Where children look changes the result
events.who: Saori Usui, Atsushi Senju, Toshikazu Hasegawa and colleagues
events.text: Yawn clips only began when a child looked at the face. With this change, children with autism caught yawns as much as other children.
events.why: Weaker attention to faces, not a missing ability, may explain earlier results.

events.title: A large study finds age matters most
events.who: Alex J. Bartholomew and Elizabeth T. Cirulli
events.where: Duke University School of Medicine, North Carolina, USA
events.text: Of 328 healthy volunteers, 68% yawned at least once while watching yawn videos. Older people caught fewer yawns. Empathy, intelligence and time of day did not explain who yawned once age was counted.
events.why: It challenged the simple idea that contagious yawning measures empathy.

events.title: A thermal window for yawning
events.who: Jorg Massen, Kim Dusch, Omar Eldakar and Andrew Gallup
events.text: In Vienna, people yawned more in summer than in winter, the opposite of Arizona. Contagious yawning was most common around 20 °C. It dropped near freezing and near body temperature.
events.why: The thermal window, not the season, fit both cities.

events.title: Wolves catch yawns from close partners
events.who: Teresa Romero, Marie Ito, Atsuko Saito and Toshikazu Hasegawa
events.where: University of Tokyo; wolves at Tama Zoological Park, Tokyo
events.text: Twelve wolves at a Tokyo zoo yawned more after another wolf yawned. They responded most to close social partners.
events.why: Dogs' wild relatives show the same social pattern.

events.title: Budgerigars: the first bird to catch yawns
events.who: Andrew Gallup and colleagues
events.where: State University of New York, USA
events.text: Sixteen budgerigars yawned about three times as often when they could see each other. They yawned about twice as often when watching a video of a yawning budgie.
events.why: It was the first experimental evidence of contagious yawning outside mammals.

events.title: Bigger brains, longer yawns
events.who: Andrew C. Gallup, A. M. Church and A. J. Pelegrino
events.text: The team timed yawns in online videos of 19 mammal species, from about 0.8 seconds in mice to about 6.5 seconds in people. Longer average yawns went with heavier brains and more cortical neurons.
events.why: If yawns cool the brain, bigger brains might need longer yawns.

events.title: Dog breeds with bigger brains yawn longer
events.who: Andrew C. Gallup, L. Moscatello and Jorg J. M. Massen
events.text: The team timed 272 yawns from 198 dogs of 23 breeds. Breed averages ran from about 1.4 to 2.8 seconds. Breeds with heavier brains yawned longer, even after body size was taken into account.
events.why: The brain-size pattern held within one species too.

events.title: Wild lions catch yawns and move together
events.who: Grazia Casetta, Andrea Paolo Nolfo and Elisabetta Palagi
events.where: University of Pisa, Italy; field site in South Africa
events.text: The team filmed 19 wild lions in South Africa for four months. A lion that saw a pride mate yawn was far more likely to yawn within three minutes. Afterwards the two often moved in step.
events.why: Catching yawns may help a group act together.

events.title: 101 species timed, birds included
events.who: Jorg Massen, Margarita Hartlieb, Andrew Gallup and colleagues
events.where: Utrecht University, University of Vienna and partners
events.text: Researchers timed 1,291 yawns from 55 mammal and 46 bird species. In both groups, bigger brains with more neurons meant longer yawns. Mammals yawned longer than birds with brains of the same size.
events.why: The link between brain and yawn length holds across warm-blooded animals.

events.title: Horses catch yawns from friends
events.who: Alice Galotti, Martina Romano, Paolo Baragli and Elisabetta Palagi
events.text: Researchers watched 48 horses on pasture. Yawns were answered far more often after a yawn than after chewing. Horses caught yawns most from kin and grooming partners.
events.why: Yawn contagion turns up in a grazing animal too.

events.title: Fetal yawns and birth weight
events.who: Damiano Menin, Paola Veronese, Maria Teresa Gervasi and colleagues
events.where: Universities of Ferrara and Padua, Italy
events.text: Ultrasound scans of 32 fetuses between 23 and 31 weeks counted under five yawns an hour on average. Fetuses that yawned more tended to have slightly lower birth weight. The authors say this needs checking.
events.why: Fetal yawning may one day help doctors check on a baby before birth.

facts: Yawning is present by the end of the first trimester, long before a baby is born.
Breathing air with over 100 times the normal carbon dioxide made people breathe harder, but not yawn more.
Covering your mouth will not stop a yawn spreading: faces with the mouth hidden were just as catching.
In one study, 30% of people who read about yawning for five minutes yawned. You may be one of them now.
Average yawns ran from about 0.8 seconds in mice to about 6.5 seconds in people in a 2016 study.
